title: MedAgents: Large Language Models as Collaborators for Zero-shot Medical Reasoning
authors: Tang X, Zou A, Zhang Z, Li Z, Zhao Y, Zhang X, Cohan A, Gerstein M
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024, pp. 599-621
published_version_checked: yes - Findings of ACL 2024 (ACL Anthology). Numbers below read from arXiv v4 HTML (2311.10537v4); not cross-checked against the Anthology PDF
metadata_verified_via: ACL Anthology (earlier session) + arXiv v4 HTML (this session)
objective: Training-free role-play multi-agent collaboration for zero-shot medical QA
architecture_methods: Decentralised role-play discussion with a summariser: (1) expert gathering, (2) individual analyses, (3) report summarisation, (4) iterative collaborative consultation until consensus, (5) decision. No external tools or retrieval.
dataset_sample: 9 datasets: MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and 6 MMLU medical subtasks (multiple-choice QA)
metrics: Accuracy; cost per 100 questions; inference time
baselines: Zero-shot, zero-shot CoT, zero-shot CoT+SC, few-shot, few-shot CoT, few-shot CoT+SC; Flan-PaLM (reported from Singhal et al.); open medical models (MedAlpaca-7B, BioMedGPT-10B, BioMedLM-2.7B, BioBERT, SciBERT, BERT). No tool/RAG or compute-matched single-agent baseline.
main_findings: GPT-4: MedAgents MedQA 83.7 vs zero-shot CoT 61.8 and zero-shot CoT+SC 74.5; MedMCQA 74.8 vs 69.0/70.1; PubMedQA 76.8 vs 71.0/75.3; 9-dataset avg 86.7 vs 80.8/83.0 (few-shot CoT+SC avg 85.4). GPT-3.5: MedQA 64.1 vs 44.3/61.3; PubMedQA 72.9 vs zero-shot CoT+SC 75.7 (MedAgents lower); avg 72.1 vs 70.9 (few-shot CoT+SC 71.6). Ablation on MedQA (base model not stated in fetched text): direct 49.0, CoT 55.0, +analysis 62.0, +summary 65.0, +consultation 67.0 - the analysis step gives the largest gain, discussion adds 2 points. ~77% of 40 sampled errors involve lack or mis-retrieval of domain knowledge. Cost about $1.41 per 100 questions; ~40 s per example.
limitations: Exam-style MCQ only; zero-shot comparison means few-shot CoT+SC nearly matches it on GPT-4 (85.4 vs 86.7); API-call counts not reported, so compute relative to CoT+SC is unknown; errors dominated by knowledge gaps that discussion cannot fix; possible contamination not addressed in fetched text; authors list outdated parametric knowledge and low-resource languages.
relevance: P4/RQ4: baselines are prompting-only and not compute-matched; ablation shows most gain comes before discussion. P3: knowledge errors suggest need for retrieval.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports role specialisation modestly; the ablation and the near-tie with few-shot CoT+SC weaken the claim that multi-round discussion itself drives gains.
claims_supported: Role-play MAS improves zero-shot medical MCQ accuracy over zero-shot CoT/CoT-SC; most errors are knowledge errors.

title: MDAgents: An Adaptive Collaboration of LLMs for Medical Decision-Making
authors: Kim Y, Park C, Jeong H, Chan YS, Xu X, McDuff D, Lee H, Ghassemi M, Breazeal C, Park HW
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024), Main Conference Track, pp. 79410-79452
published_version_checked: yes - NeurIPS 2024 (proceedings page, earlier session); numbers read from arXiv v3 HTML
metadata_verified_via: NeurIPS proceedings page (earlier session) + arXiv 2404.15155v3 HTML (this session, first 100k chars)
objective: Adaptively assign solo vs group collaboration by case complexity
architecture_methods: LLM complexity classifier routes to: low = single primary-care agent; moderate = multidisciplinary team with moderator; high = integrated care team (hierarchical). Moderator review and external medical knowledge (MedRAG) in group mode.
models_tools: GPT-4(V) for all benchmarks except MedVidQA (Gemini-Pro(Vision)); other models in appendix tables (not read)
dataset_sample: 10 benchmarks: MedQA, PubMedQA, DDXPlus, SymCat, JAMA, MedBullets, Path-VQA, PMC-VQA, MIMIC-CXR, MedVidQA; evaluation on sampled subsets (50 samples per dataset for timing)
metrics: Accuracy (mean +/- SD over runs); inference time by complexity level
baselines: Single-agent: zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, CoT-SC, Ensemble Refinement, Medprompt. Group: majority voting, weighted voting, Borda count, MedAgents, Meta-Prompting, ReConcile, AutoGen, DyLAN.
main_findings: Best on 7/10 benchmarks; up to +4.2% over previous best (p<0.05) (abstract). MedQA 88.7+/-4.0 vs best single CoT-SC 83.9+/-2.7 and best group ReConcile 81.3+/-3.0. PubMedQA 75.0 vs ReConcile 79.7 (group baseline better). MedVidQA 56.2+/-6.7 vs weighted voting 57.8. Moderator review + external knowledge: +11.8% average accuracy (abstract; components combined). Average inference time per case: low 14.7 s, moderate 95.5 s, high 226 s.
limitations: Small evaluation subsets with large SDs (e.g., +/-4.0 on MedQA); RAG and moderator gains reported together (confounded); whether single-agent baselines had RAG not verified; cost comparison in Appendix D.2 not read; benchmark QA only.
relevance: P4/RQ4: broadest baseline set among clinical MAS, but tool/retrieval and compute not matched; routing to a single agent for simple cases implies MAS is not always needed.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports adaptive/centralised moderation; also shows a strong single-agent baseline (CoT-SC) beats several group methods on MedQA.
claims_supported: Adaptive complexity routing with a moderator achieved best results on 7/10 medical benchmarks at higher latency.

title: Mitigating Cognitive Biases in Clinical Decision-Making Through Multi-Agent Conversations Using Large Language Models: Simulation Study
authors: Ke Y, Yang R, Lie SA, Lim TXY, Ning Y, Li I, Abdullah HR, Ting DSW, Liu N
published_version_checked: yes - JMIR 2024 (preprint arXiv 2401.14589)
metadata_verified_via: JMIR article page (earlier session, full text)
objective: Test whether multi-agent conversations with a devil's-advocate role reduce anchoring/confirmation bias in diagnosis
architecture_methods: Decentralised conversation (Microsoft AutoGen) among role agents plus a recorder; Framework 3: two residents (one devil's advocate) + recorder; Framework 4: + expert; Framework 4-C: senior doctor explicitly addressing cognitive biases
dataset_sample: 16 cases (15 published case reports with cognitive-bias errors, selected from 37 eligible, + 1 unpublished); 5 runs per framework (80 responses each)
metrics: Initial and final diagnosis accuracy; odds ratios
baselines: Initial (single-pass) diagnosis; 3 human doctors (>=5 years experience)
main_findings: Initial diagnosis 0/80 correct in all frameworks. Final accuracy 51/80 (64%) F3, 55/80 (69%) F4, 61/80 (76%) F4-C. Humans 13/48 (27%) initial, 23/48 (48%) final. F4-C OR 3.49 (p=.002); F4 OR 2.39 (p=.03); F3 p=.10.
limitations: 16 published cases (possible training-data contamination); images excluded; selection bias; team size not literature-based; a fifth agent did not participate effectively; no single-agent self-critique or compute-matched baseline.
relevance: P1/P2, RQ1: closest analogue to a critic role; P4: baseline is single-pass, not a self-critique single agent.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports critic/devil's-advocate roles for anchoring; does not test whether a single agent prompted to self-critique would do as well.
claims_supported: A bias-aware senior/devil's advocate role raised final-diagnosis accuracy to 76% on 16 bias-prone cases.

title: One is Not Enough: Multi-Agent Conversation Framework Enhances Rare Disease Diagnostic Capabilities of Large Language Models
authors: Li J, Chen X, Liu W, Wang L, Guo Y, You M, et al.
published_version_checked: likely the earlier version of chen2025mac (npj Digit Med 2025), but sample (150 diseases vs 302 cases), agent count (3 doctors + supervisor vs 4 + supervisor) and baselines differ; do not cite these numbers for the npj paper

architecture_methods: 3 doctor agents + 1 supervising agent in AutoGen
dataset_sample: 150 rare diseases (normalised random sampling); initial presentations manually extracted by clinicians
metrics: Exact-match most likely diagnosis; possible diagnoses containing correct answer; 0-5 diagnosis closeness scale; helpfulness of further tests; Likert knowledge ratings (3 blinded physicians)
baselines: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 input-output prompting; zero-shot CoT, tree-of-thoughts, reflections-of-thoughts (no numbers in main text)
main_findings: Initial presentation, most likely dx: GPT-3.5 16.5%, GPT-4 19.5%, MAC 28%; possible dx 28.3% / 31.1% / 47.3%; further tests 67.3% / 70.7% / 83.3%. Complete presentation, most likely dx 27.3% / 32.2% / 48.0%; possible dx 41.6% / 41.9% / 66.7%. Prompting techniques gave no diagnostic improvement (main text, numbers in supplement not read).

supports_or_contradicts: Supports MAS gains over single-pass GPT-4 but absolute accuracy is low and baselines are weak.
claims_supported: (Preprint) MAC raised most-likely-diagnosis accuracy from 19.5% to 28% (initial) and 32.2% to 48.0% (complete) vs single GPT-4.

title: Tiered Agentic Oversight: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent System for Healthcare Safety
authors: Kim Y, Jeong H, Park C, Park E, Zhang H, Liu X, Lee H, McDuff D, Ghassemi M, Breazeal C, Tulebaev S, Park HW
venue: arXiv preprint 2506.12482 (v2, 2025-09-28); an ICML 2025 virtual page (icml.cc/virtual/2025/49358) with a variant title appeared in search results but was not opened - likely a workshop presentation, unconfirmed
published_version_checked: no - ICML 2025 listing seen but not verified
objective: Hierarchical, escalation-based multi-agent oversight for healthcare safety
architecture_methods: Agent Recruiter selects medical/ethical roles; Agent Router assigns agents to tiers 1-3; each agent outputs risk level and escalation flag; intra- and inter-tier discussion; disagreement triggers escalation; Final Decision Agent weights higher tiers; human clinician review is top escalation path
models_tools: Gemini-2.0 Flash, Gemini-2.5 Pro and others
dataset_sample: SafetyBench, MedSafetyBench, LLM Red-teaming, Medical Triage, MM-SafetyBench (health consultation); clinician study: 5 physicians, 20 real triage scenarios
metrics: Accuracy; harmfulness score; proportion appropriate; attribute-dependent triage accuracy; 100 - attack success rate; cost (USD); error absorption/amplification
baselines: Single-agent: zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, Multi-role (one LLM simulating all tiers), Safety Prompt. Multi-agent: majority voting, LLM-Debate, MedAgents, AutoDefense. Adaptive: MDAgents.
main_findings: Claims best on 4/5 benchmarks, up to +8.2% over strongest baseline (Red Teaming, Gemini-2.0 Flash); Gemini-2.5 Pro table shows positive gain over second-best on all 5 (e.g., +4.00 Red Teaming, +4.90 Medical Triage) - internally inconsistent with '4 of 5'. Removing Tier 1 agents causes largest drop; adaptive tiering beats all-Tier-1/2/3. Absorbs 16.9-24.3% of individual agent errors; error amplification <8.4%. Clinician study: doctor feedback raised TAO from 40% (8/20) to 60% (12/20); unaided doctors 51.8%; ICC 0.610 (oversight necessity), 0.259 (appropriateness), -0.101 (safety confidence). TAO cost listed 55.2 USD in the Gemini-2.5 Pro setting.
limitations: Modest gains, 3 seeds, no significance tests; small clinician panel with poor agreement; benchmark-based safety, not real deployment; centralised router a single point of failure.
relevance: P2/RQ1: escalation and human-in-the-loop evaluated; P4/RQ4: includes a single-LLM 'Multi-role' baseline - partial isolation of multi-agent structure from role-play; cost reported.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports escalation tiers and human handoff; clinician study shows the system alone (40%) underperformed unaided doctors (51.8%).
claims_supported: (Preprint) Tiered escalation MAS was best on most safety benchmarks against single-agent, multi-role and MAS baselines; with clinician feedback accuracy rose 40% to 60% on 20 triage cases.

relevance: P1/RQ1: static QA overstates readiness; used as environment for later agent systems.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports P1; not a MAS-vs-single comparison of doctor agents.
claims_supported: (Preprint) Sequential diagnosis accuracy can fall below one-tenth of static accuracy.

title: The Optimization Paradox in Clinical AI Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Bedi S, Mlauzi I, Shin D, Koyejo S, Shah NH
published_version_checked: no - no journal-ref (checked 2026-11-27)
objective: Compare single- vs multi-agent pipelines on real patient data and test whether best components make the best system
architecture_methods: Diagnosis decomposed into information gathering, interpretation, differential diagnosis; single model for all vs specialised model per stage; 'Best of Breed' assembled from top components
dataset_sample: 2,400 real patient cases from MIMIC-CDM; appendicitis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis
metrics: Diagnostic accuracy; process adherence; cost efficiency
baselines: Single-agent systems
main_findings: MAS generally outperformed single-agent systems; Best-of-Breed system: 85.5% information-gathering accuracy but 67.7% diagnostic accuracy, vs 77.4% for the top multi-agent system.
limitations: Preprint; four abdominal conditions; abstract only.
relevance: P4/RQ4: real-data single vs MAS comparison; component metrics do not predict system performance - supports end-to-end and ablation evaluation.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports MAS on real data but shows composition effects; argues against component-only validation.
claims_supported: (Preprint) On 2,400 MIMIC-CDM cases, best components gave 67.7% vs 77.4% for the best integrated MAS.

title: ConfAgents: A Conformal-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Cost-Efficient Medical Diagnosis
authors: Zhao H, Zhu Y, Wang Z, Wang Y, Gao J, Ma L
published_version_checked: no - no venue stated in PDF read
objective: Use conformal prediction to escalate only uncertain cases to multi-agent RAG collaboration
architecture_methods: MainAgent answer distribution; CP Judger with per-query calibration set (N similar questions), nonconformity 1-p, alpha=0.05; singleton set -> answer directly, else AssistAgents run iterative RAG (Merck Manual, k=3, up to 3 iterations)
dataset_sample: MedQA, MMLU medical, MedBullets, AfriMedQA; Test-Hard and Test-Normal subsets of 100 each (MedAgentsBench protocol)
metrics: Accuracy; processing time; completion and total tokens; Balanced Efficiency Score
baselines: Single-agent zero-shot, few-shot, self-consistency; MAS MedAgents, ReConcile, MDAgents, ColaCare
main_findings: MedQA GPT-4o: ConfAgents 80.21% at 9.11 s vs MDAgents 75.10% at 25.15 s (~2.76x faster, ~2.01x fewer completion tokens, 1.22x fewer total tokens) and MedAgents 78.80% at 70.21 s (~7.71x faster). Abstract claims >50% compute reduction on MedQA.
limitations: Preprint; 100-question subsets; inconsistency (80.21% in Table 2 vs 77.00% in Table 6); MCQ only.
relevance: P2/RQ4: uncertainty-triggered escalation; reports tokens and time against MAS baselines.
supports_or_contradicts: Suggests much MAS compute is unnecessary for confident cases; supports gating MAS by uncertainty.
claims_supported: (Preprint) Conformal gating matched or beat MDAgents/MedAgents with 2.8-7.7x less time on MedQA.

title: AI Agents in Clinical Medicine: A Systematic Review
authors: Gorenshtein A, Omar M, Glicksberg BS, Nadkarni GN, Klang E
published_version_checked: no - Sciety showed no journal version (earlier session); PMC record PMC12407621 not reachable (reCAPTCHA) this session
objective: Systematically review LLM agents (tool use and/or multi-agent) on clinical tasks with quantitative baselines
architecture_methods: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, citation chasing, preprint servers; 2022-10-01 to 2025-08-05; PROSPERO CRD420251120318
dataset_sample: 6,023 records; 254 full texts; 20 included
metrics: Gain over baseline LLM; study design; data type
baselines: Baseline LLMs in included studies
main_findings: Median gain +36% over baseline LLM (range +3.5% to +76%); single-agent tool calling median +53.0% (IQR 36.0-56.9); multi-agent without tools +14.05% (IQR 8.95-45.15); multi-agent with tools +17.17% (IQR 4.12-39.3). 13/20 (65%) synthetic data; real patient data in 2 studies (117 patients); all single-centre; 1 RCT; GPT-4 family in 15 (75%). 'No study provides a comparison of multi-agent to single-agent.' Inverted-U by agent count, best at 4-5 agents.
limitations: Exclusion counts sum to 237 vs 234 expected; no meta-analysis; heterogeneous tasks; preprint.
relevance: P4/RQ4: core evidence that MAS vs single-agent comparisons are missing and real data are rare.
supports_or_contradicts: Gives no support for MAS superiority; median gains larger for single-agent tool calling (not head-to-head).
claims_supported: (Preprint) Among 20 clinical agent studies, none compared MAS with single agents; 65% used synthetic data.

title: Artificial intelligence agents in healthcare research: A scoping review
authors: Njei B, Al-Ajlouni YA, Kanmounye US, Boateng S, Nguefang GL, Njei N, Hamouri S, Al-Ajlouni AF
published_version_checked: yes - PLoS One 2026 (PMID 41666194)
objective: Scoping review of AI agents in healthcare research
architecture_methods: Arksey and O'Malley; PRISMA-ScR; PubMed, Web of Science, arXiv, medRxiv; Jan 2015 - Dec 7 2025; no risk-of-bias assessment; no protocol registration
dataset_sample: 1,070 records; 324 full texts; 43 included (36 from 2025)
metrics: System type, evaluation setting, outcomes
main_findings: 8 conversational, 17 workflow/automation, 18 multimodal decision-support agents (abstract); Table 1 lists 44 rows (~21 labelled LLM-based multi-agent, by this researcher's count). Evaluation mostly simulated or laboratory, few clinical pilots; clinical outcomes and safety endpoints rarely addressed; human evaluations small and rarely by practising clinicians; one RCT found low physician engagement due to usability; latency up to 4.7 s per query reported.
limitations: Scoping design, includes preprints, no quality appraisal; internal count inconsistency (43 vs 44 rows; type labels do not match 8/17/18).
relevance: P4: peer-reviewed confirmation that evaluation is mostly simulated and safety endpoints rare.
supports_or_contradicts: Supports P4 gap; notes some MAS triage systems beat single agents (not traced).
claims_supported: Peer-reviewed scoping review (43 studies): evaluation mostly simulated; safety endpoints rarely addressed.
